title: Concurrency in Python: threads, locks and the GIL
seriesTitle: Python: threading, the GIL and asyncio
seriesDescription: Threads, locks, the GIL, concurrent.futures, asyncio, queues and classic drills. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Thread lifecycle, GIL limits, Lock versus RLock, Event, Condition and Semaphore, atomicity of +=, check-then-act races, lazy initialisation and thread exceptions.
source: Python docs: threading, GIL glossary, concurrent.futures; PEP 703 and PEP 779 (free-threaded CPython); Real Python threading guides; GeeksforGeeks; InterviewBit multithreading lists

questions.prompt: In CPython, a thread that is blocked waiting on a network socket releases the GIL, so Python threads can overlap I/O waits and speed up I/O-bound programs.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: blocking I/O calls release the GIL, so other threads run while one waits.

options.text: False
options.why: The GIL is released around blocking system calls, so threading does help I/O-bound code.

questions.explanation: The GIL only stops two threads executing Python bytecode at the same instant. Waiting on I/O is not executing bytecode, so threads still overlap waits. (Free-threaded CPython without a GIL, PEP 703, was experimental in 3.13 and became an officially supported but still optional separate build in 3.14 via PEP 779; the default build keeps the GIL.)

questions.prompt: A Python service must hash 4 GB of files on an 8-core machine using pure-Python-heavy CPU work. Which approach gives the best speed-up in standard CPython?

options.text: Split the files across a ProcessPoolExecutor with about 8 workers.
options.why: Correct: each process has its own interpreter and its own GIL, so work runs on all cores.

options.text: Start 8 threading.Thread workers, one per core, and join them all at the end.
options.why: Threads share one GIL, so CPU-bound bytecode still runs on one core at a time.

options.text: Run the hashing in 8 asyncio tasks gathered together on one event loop.
options.why: asyncio is cooperative on a single thread; CPU work never yields, so it is no faster.

options.text: Lower sys.setswitchinterval so threads swap more often.
options.why: A shorter switch interval only adds overhead; it does not allow parallel bytecode execution.

questions.explanation: CPU-bound work needs processes (multiprocessing, ProcessPoolExecutor), a native extension that releases the GIL, or a free-threaded build. Note hashlib releases the GIL for large buffers, a nuance worth mentioning.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: In CPython, several threads running counter += 1 on a shared int can lose updates even though the GIL exists.
questions.reason: The GIL can hand control to another thread between the bytecodes that load, add and store the value.

whys.a: Correct: += compiles to separate load, add, store steps and a thread switch between them loses an update, which is exactly why the GIL does not make it safe.
whys.b: R is the actual mechanism behind A, so "true but not the explanation" understates it.
whys.c: R is true: bytecode-level switching between load, add and store is real, so R is not false.
whys.d: A is true, not false: GIL protects the interpreter internals, not your read-modify-write sequences.

questions.explanation: The GIL protects CPython's internals. Compound operations such as +=, check-then-set on a dict, or append-after-length-check are not atomic. Use threading.Lock or a queue.

questions.prompt: Write a Python class Account with self.balance = 0, a threading.Lock stored on the instance, and a method withdraw(amount) that returns False if funds are insufficient and otherwise subtracts the amount and returns True. The check and the subtraction must be atomic.
questions.explanation: Checking the balance outside the lock and subtracting inside it is still a check-then-act race. Use a context manager so the lock is released on every return path and exception.

questions.prompt:
Many threads run the code below against a shared dict cache. Which statement is accurate?

if key not in cache:
    cache[key] = compute(key)
return cache[key]

Pick one.

options.text: compute(key) can run twice for one key, as check and store are separate steps.
options.why: Correct: two threads can both see the key missing and both compute; each dict operation is atomic but the sequence is not.

options.text: It is safe, because every single dict operation is atomic under the GIL, so no lock is needed.
options.why: Individual operations are atomic, but the two-step check-then-act is not.

options.text: It raises RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration, because cache is being modified.
options.why: That error appears when iterating while mutating; there is no iteration here.

options.text: It is safe as long as compute is a pure function without any side effects or shared state.
options.why: Purity avoids wrong values but not duplicate work or the race itself.

questions.explanation: Guard the whole sequence with a Lock (or use a per-key lock, or functools.lru_cache for pure functions). Check-then-act on a shared dict is the classic race.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: A Python threading.Lock can be released by a thread other than the one that acquired it.
questions.reason: A Python threading.RLock must be released by the thread that owns it.

whys.a: Not chosen: both statements are true, but R describes the contrast case and does not explain why Lock has no owner.
whys.b: Correct: both are true (Lock is a plain binary semaphore-like primitive with no owner, RLock records its owner and a recursion count), but R is a contrast rather than the explanation. Verified by running it.
whys.c: Not chosen: R is true; releasing an RLock from another thread raises RuntimeError.
whys.d: Not chosen: A is true; another thread may call release() on a locked Lock.

questions.explanation: Use RLock for re-entrant code (a thread may acquire it again); a second acquire() of a plain Lock by the same thread deadlocks. Verified by running it.

questions.prompt:
What does this Python snippet print?

threading.Thread(target=lambda: print(threading.current_thread().name), name="worker").run()

What is printed?

options.text: MainThread, because run() executes on the calling thread
options.why: Correct: run() is an ordinary method call, so the target executes on the caller, the main thread (verified by running it).

options.text: worker, the name that was given to the thread you created
options.why: The name belongs to a thread that was never started; run() does not create one.

options.text: Thread-1, the default name given to every newly created thread
options.why: Thread-1 is the default name only for a thread created without a name, and none starts here.

options.text: Nothing, because the thread object was never started
options.why: run() executes the body synchronously, so it prints before the statement finishes.

questions.explanation: start() creates the OS thread, which then calls run(). Calling run() yourself is a plain call, a favourite interview trap.

questions.prompt: Match each threading primitive with the behaviour that identifies it.

right.text: A second acquire() by the thread that already holds it blocks forever
May be acquired again by its owner, tracked with a recursion count
A flag that any number of threads can wait on until another thread sets it
Lets threads wait for a predicate and be notified, always used with a lock
Allows up to three threads inside the guarded section at once
Runs a function in a separate worker process

questions.explanation: Lock and RLock give mutual exclusion; Event is a broadcast flag; Condition adds wait/notify around shared state; Semaphore counts permits. Worker processes belong to multiprocessing.

questions.prompt: Four threads each execute counter += 1 250 times on a shared module-level int that starts at 0, with no lock. What is the largest final value that is possible?
questions.explanation: Each increment adds at most 1, and there are 4 x 250 = 1000 increments, so 1000 is the upper bound. Lost updates only make the result smaller. The interview point: += is load, add, store, not atomic, even with a GIL.

questions.prompt: Write a Python class Counter with self.count starting at 0, a method increment() and a method get(), made thread-safe with a threading.Lock.
questions.explanation: Both methods use the same lock. Reading under the lock is optional for a plain int in CPython but keeps the class correct on free-threaded builds and for compound reads. An itertools.count or a queue is another style.

questions.prompt: Given a threading.Lock named lock, write a snippet that tries to acquire it for at most 1 second, runs do_work() only if it got the lock, and always releases it.
questions.explanation: acquire(timeout=1) returns False when it gives up. The try starts only after a successful acquire, otherwise you would release a lock you do not hold (RuntimeError). Plain "with lock:" cannot time out.

questions.prompt: Select all true statements about threading.Lock and threading.RLock.

options.text: An RLock can be acquired again by the thread that already holds it without blocking
options.why: Correct: it counts the recursion depth and is free again after the matching number of release() calls.

options.text: A plain Lock acquired twice by the same thread blocks that thread forever
options.why: Correct: Lock has no owner, so the second acquire waits for a release that never comes.

options.text: lock.acquire(timeout=2) returns False if the lock was not obtained in time
options.why: Correct: the return value tells you whether you hold the lock.

options.text: A Lock is released automatically as soon as the thread holding it ends
options.why: Wrong: a dead thread leaves the lock held; always release in finally or use with.

options.text: An RLock may be released by any thread, not only by the one that acquired it
options.why: Wrong: releasing an RLock you do not own raises RuntimeError.

questions.explanation: Use RLock for code paths that re-enter (recursion, methods calling each other under the same lock); prefer a plain Lock otherwise because it is cheaper and catches accidental re-entry as a hang you can see.

questions.prompt:
This lazy initialiser is called from many threads.

_inst = None
_lock = threading.Lock()
def get_config():
    global _inst
    if _inst is None:
        with _lock:
            _inst = load_config()
    return _inst

Which statement identifies the bug?

options.text: The global statement gives every thread its own private copy of _inst, so sharing fails.
options.why: Globals are shared by all threads; thread-local data needs threading.local.

options.text: The with statement releases the lock before the assignment to _inst is executed.
options.why: The lock is held for the whole indented block, including the assignment.

options.text: No second check inside the lock, so several threads each run load_config.
options.why: Correct: threads that passed the first test queue on the lock and then each run load_config; the last one wins.

options.text: A Lock created at module level cannot be shared safely between several threads.
options.why: A module-level lock is the normal way to share one.

questions.explanation: Fix: re-test "if _inst is None" inside the with block (double-checked locking), or build the object at import time, or use functools.cache on a zero-argument function.

questions.prompt: Complete the sentences about the threading module.
questions.text: Calling {1}() runs the target in a new thread, while calling run() executes it on the caller. {2}() blocks the caller until that thread finishes. A thread created with {3}=True does not keep the interpreter alive at exit.
questions.explanation: A non-daemon thread keeps the process running until it ends; daemon threads are stopped abruptly at shutdown, so do not rely on them to flush data. There is no kill() for threads: signal them with an Event.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: An exception that escapes a thread target does not propagate to the thread that started it.
questions.reason: Thread.join() re-raises the exception from the target in the calling thread.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot be the explanation.
whys.b: R is false, so option b (both true) is wrong.
whys.c: Correct: the traceback is printed by the thread excepthook and the main thread carries on (verified by running it); join() only waits, so R is false.
whys.d: A is true, so option d (A false) is wrong.

questions.explanation: To get the exception back, catch it in the target and hand it over through a queue, or use ThreadPoolExecutor, whose Future.result() re-raises it.

questions.prompt: Calling time.sleep(1) inside a "with lock:" block releases the lock for that second so other threads can enter.

options.text: True
options.why: Wrong: sleep never releases any lock; other threads keep waiting.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: sleeping while holding a lock keeps everyone else out for the whole second (verified: a non-blocking acquire fails meanwhile).

questions.explanation: Only Condition.wait() releases its lock while waiting. Never sleep or do I/O inside a critical section unless you must.
